parts.title: Campus Conversation: A Problem in the Dorm Room
script: Listen to a conversation between a student and a woman who works at the campus housing office.
Hi there. Welcome to the housing office. How can I help you?
Hi. My name is David Park. I live in Hill Hall, room two-fourteen. The heater in my room is not working.
Oh no. When did it stop working?
Three days ago. At night my room is very cold. Last night I slept in my jacket.
That sounds terrible. Did you tell anyone before today?
Yes, I told my resident assistant, the student who helps on my floor. She said I should come here and fill out a form.
She was right. Here is the repair form. Please write your name, your room number, and the problem.
OK. Do I need to pay for the repair?
No, no. Repairs in the dorms are free for students.
That's good to hear. How long will it take?
Usually two or three days. But because it is a heater, and it's cold outside, we will send someone tomorrow morning.
Tomorrow morning? Great. But I have a chemistry class at nine. Do I need to be in my room?
No, you don't. The repair worker has a key. He can go in when you are not there.
OK. And what can I do tonight? It's really cold.
We have extra blankets here. You can take one now and bring it back after the repair.
Perfect. I'll take one. Thank you so much.

parts.title: Academic Lecture: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?
script: Listen to part of a lecture in an astronomy class.
OK, everyone, let's begin. Today's topic is the Moon. More exactly, why the Moon seems to change its shape during the month.
First, an important fact. The Moon does not make its own light. It is not like the Sun. The light we see from the Moon is sunlight. The Sun shines on the Moon, and the Moon reflects that light to us.

The Sun always lights up one half of the Moon. But the Moon moves around the Earth. It takes about twenty-nine days to go around one time. So, as it moves, we see different amounts of the bright half. These different shapes are called phases.
Let's look at the main phases. When the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, the bright side faces away from us. We can't see the Moon at all. This is called the new moon.

After that, we see a thin piece of light, like a smile. This is a crescent. Then, after about one week, we see half of the Moon. And about two weeks after the new moon, we see the whole bright side. A big round circle. That's the full moon.
Then the bright part gets smaller again, until it is a new moon one more time. And the cycle starts again.

Now, many people think the phases happen because the Earth's shadow covers the Moon. But that's not true. The Earth's shadow only falls on the Moon during an eclipse, and eclipses are rare. Phases happen every month.
So here is some homework. Tonight, go outside and look at the Moon. Draw its shape. Do this for one week, and bring your drawings to class next Thursday.
